title: Accelerated search for global extrema in structured quantum signals
authors: Sachin S. Bharadwaj, Katepalli R. Sreenivasan
abstract: Extreme values of a physical system are rare by definition, yet they can govern some of its most consequential and anomalous behavior. Their sparsity makes them particularly costly to identify in large data sets. Quantum computation offers a potential way to reduce this cost. The challenge is that quantum amplitudes cannot simply be read, copied, compared, or marked using conventional search oracles. Here we introduce an algorithm for searching amplitude-encoded quantum signals that exploits their underlying structure. Through a nonlinear amplitude transformation, the algorithm identifies and certifies a global extremum while exponentially reducing the effective search space for structured signals. We establish a polylogarithmic query complexity in the data size $N$, together with global completeness, efficient classical verification, and a measurable criterion for quantifying exploitable structure. We demonstrate the framework using computational turbulence data. Applied to line cuts of velocity gradients from a $1024^3$ simulation containing more than one billion grid points, the algorithm consistently isolates the extreme tail and reduces the median search space to $O(\log N)$. The clustered structure characteristic of turbulence further accelerates the search. These results establish a direct connection between physical structure and quantum advantage in extreme-value search. For accessibility, the main text emphasizes the central ideas and results, while the theoretical derivations are provided in the Appendices.
summary: This work presents a quantum algorithm to efficiently locate global extrema in highly structured quantum signals, such as those found in turbulent fluid dynamics. By employing a nonlinear amplitude transformation, the search complexity is reduced to polylogarithmic scaling, demonstrating a direct quantum advantage derived from the physical structure of the data. This advances the field by connecting physical structure to quantum computational resource bounds.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of finding global extrema in structured quantum signals when the data are encoded in quantum amplitudes that cannot be read or compared conventionally.
main_result: An algorithm is proposed that achieves polylogarithmic query complexity in the data size N by exploiting the underlying structure of the signal via a nonlinear amplitude transformation.
method: The core method involves a two-stage quantum process: an approximate filtering stage using a Chebyshev-walk nonlinear transformation to suppress background noise, followed by a certification stage to locate the extremum.
model_or_system: The framework is tested on signals derived from computational turbulence data (Navier-Stokes equations), where the data are represented by normalized amplitudes of an n-qubit quantum state.
key_observables: Structure Factor ($S_{in}$), Query Complexity ($Q_{e2e} = 	ext{polylog}(N)$), and the probability mass retained in the filtered tail ($P_R$).
important_parameters: The complexity scales polylogarithmically with N, significantly beating classical O(N) and standard quantum O(sqrt(N)) search bounds.
main_assumptions: The algorithm assumes access only to state-preparation circuits and relies on the physical structure being sufficiently rare and concentrated to allow for effective filtering.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the end-to-end workflow, showing the sequence from calibration through the nonlinear filtering stage to the final candidate recovery and certification.
paper_structure: The paper details the theoretical framework, introducing the nonlinear amplitude transformation (QG1) for filtering, establishing the complexity bounds for global completeness, and providing appendices for detailed theoretical derivations related to PDE-to-Extremum mapping.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum algorithms, the connection between physical structure (like turbulence intermittency) and the required quantum resources provides a novel theoretical link between condensed matter/fluid dynamics and quantum computation complexity.
